title: Your First-Aid Kit

learn.summary: A kit you've assembled yourself beats a store-bought one you've never opened, because building it teaches you what's inside and why. The Red Cross publishes a recommended contents list for a family of four; the real differentiator isn't contents anyway — it's whether the kit is findable in 10 seconds and audited twice a year.

do: Tell everyone in your household where the first-aid kit lives (or will live), and put it in that one consistent spot today.

children.title: Building a Home Kit

learn.summary: The Red Cross family-of-four baseline: assorted adhesive bandages, sterile gauze pads (3x3 and 4x4) and roller gauze, adhesive tape, elastic bandage, antiseptic wipes, antibiotic ointment, hydrocortisone cream, tweezers, scissors, nitrile gloves (2+ pairs), an instant cold pack, a digital thermometer, an emergency blanket, and a first-aid guide. Store it in a labeled, waterproof container where adults can grab it fast but small children can't.

do: Inventory your current supplies against that list this week and buy the missing items in one order — total cost is typically under $40.

children.title: Car & Travel Kits

learn.summary: Your car kit handles two scenarios the home kit doesn't: roadside trauma (add a flashlight, reflective triangle, emergency blanket, and heavier gauze) and being stranded (water, snacks, phone charger, seasonal layers). Heat is the enemy — car interiors exceed 60°C (140°F) in summer, degrading medications and adhesives, so audit car kits more often and skip storing heat-sensitive meds there. A pocket-sized pouch of bandages, wipes, and pain reliever covers 95% of travel needs.

do: Assemble a minimal car kit this weekend: bandages, gauze, gloves, flashlight, water bottle, and a blanket in one zip bag in the trunk.

children.title: Medication Basics Awareness

learn.summary: A sensible OTC lineup: acetaminophen and ibuprofen (they work differently and can be alternated for fever under guidance), an antihistamine like diphenhydramine or cetirizine for allergic reactions, aspirin (for the heart-attack scenario), ORS sachets, and an antacid. Awareness only — read labels, respect max daily doses (acetaminophen's 4 g adult ceiling hides in many combination cold products), and ask a pharmacist about interactions with anything prescribed. Pharmacists are the most underused free medical resource in the country.

do: Next pharmacy visit, ask the pharmacist one real question about interactions between your household's medications — it's free and they're glad to answer.

children.title: Expiry Audits

learn.summary: Adhesives dry out, ointments separate, and medications lose potency past expiry — a kit that's 5 years stale is a false sense of security. The habit that works: audit twice a year on a memorable trigger, the same clock-change weekends used for smoke-alarm batteries. Check dates, replace anything used or expired, and take expired meds to a pharmacy take-back rather than the trash or toilet.

do: Set two recurring calendar reminders right now — 'Audit first-aid kit + smoke alarms' — on the spring and fall clock-change weekends.
